newsitem.title: POLAND: Clinton leaves Poland after giving it a NATO push.
newsitem.headline: Clinton leaves Poland after giving it a NATO push.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton left Warsaw on Friday after a brief, spectacular visit designed to give Poland a helpful push on the last hard leg of its road to NATO membership.

Having chosen Warsaw as the place to celebrate this week's decision to invite Poles, Czechs and Hungarians to start NATO entry talks, Clinton flew to Romania to reassure one of the countries left out for now.

"Poland is taking its place in the community of democracy. Never again will your fate be decided by others. Never again will the birthright of freedom be denied you," Clinton told a flag-waving crowd of thousands on a Warsaw square on Thursday.
"Poland is coming home!" he told Poland, which with 38 million people is the largest country in Central Europe, and which only escaped Soviet-imposed communist rule in 1989.
Clinton is a firm advocate of admitting to NATO the three ex-communist countries leading their region's reforms.

But the U.S. Senate must next year ratify the process by a two-thirds majority before Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic can join as planned in 1999. This is by no means sure to pass, as many senators have doubts over the costs and wisdom of NATO enlargement.

"Let us not waste this unique great opportunity we have got and the support which the President of the United States has personally offered us," Trybuna daily, which supports the main ruling party of ex-communists, commented on Friday.
Speeches by Clinton and Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski on Thursday were clearly aimed at overcoming doubts among some U.S. senators over the move's cost and wisdom.

"To the citizens of my own country I say...by expanding NATO, we will help to prevent another war involving Poland, another war in Europe, another war that also claims the lives of Americans," Clinton said.
He told the NATO entrants they would have to shoulder a heavy burden, including the costs of modernising their armies. Polish leaders said they would, although no figures were published.
Kwasniewski also appealed to U.S. taxpayers.
"We thank America, we thank American taxpayers who know that no price can be placed on the peace, freedom, security and welfare of ourselves, our children and grandchildren," he said.
Clinton addressed all the objections to Poland's NATO entry raised at various times in the United States.
For those who say it might antagonise Russia, which views a larger NATO as against its interests, Clinton told the Poles they should continue to reach out to Russia.

He stressed the importance of Poland's role in providing support and encouragement to a reforming, independent Ukraine, which is also a key element of U.S. foreign policy, and said the three NATO entrants were leading the way in their region.

The Polish ex-communists, in government since 1993, were late converts to the country's NATO drive. But they hope to benefit from its success in elections on September 21, when they face a challenge from an alliance led by the Solidarity trade union.

On Friday, however, they faced heavy opposition criticism over their handling of floods sweeping southern Poland, a disaster which in Polish news media took precedence over the Clinton visit preoccupying ruling politicians this week.
